raw_response:
I'm a 50-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, Hebei. I've been farming for 20 years, and I finished junior high school, so I can read a bit and I've picked up some things from the extension office over the years, but mostly I go by what I've seen with my own eyes and what the neighbors do. My family has four people, but my son works in a factory in Handan and only comes back for busy seasons, so day-to-day it's mostly me and my wife. My daughter-in-law helps when she can, but she's got her own job in town. We have 16.1 mu total — not a big farm, not tiny either.

I've got two blocks of land. The 10 mu near the well on the flat land, that's my wheat-maize double crop. The other 6.1 mu on the south side, that's been cotton for years. I keep it because cotton prices have been decent and it's good to not put all my eggs in one basket, but honestly the picking is killing us — that's why I won't expand it beyond those 6 mu.

**Winter wheat** — I planted it last October 10th, same week as always. I used about 30 jin of seed per mu, the local variety that's reliable. Before planting I did rotary tillage and put down about 100 jin per mu of compound fertilizer as basal — the 15-15-15 kind from the dealer. The extension guy told me last year I could cut back to 80 jin, but I tried that on 2 mu and the yield dropped, so this year I'm back to my usual 100 jin. Now it's early spring and the wheat is greening up. I'll topdress with urea at jointing — about 40 jin per mu. For water, I'll irrigate three times: once at green-up if the rain doesn't come, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I used to do four, but the water fees keep going up and the well isn't as strong as it used to be, so I cut the overwintering one. I expect about 420 kg per mu if the weather cooperates — last year I got 400, the year before 450.

**Summer maize** — This goes in right after wheat harvest, around June 10th to 12th. The window is tight, sometimes only five or six days, so I use no-tillage. I hire the seeding machine and put down hybrid seed, usually Denghai or something similar, about 1.2 packages per mu. I buy the seed new every year — never save maize seed, that's just asking for trouble. At planting I put compound fertilizer down with the seed, about 100 jin per mu of the high-N kind. Then at the big trumpet stage in July, I topdress with urea. I'll irrigate twice if July and August are dry — that's usually enough for maize. I spray herbicide once and insecticide once or twice depending on whether I see corn borers. Yield should be around 450 kg per mu, maybe 500 if we get good rain.

**Cotton** — I plant around April 20th. I rotary till first, then put down basal compound fertilizer, about 80 jin per mu. I use an improved variety, Guoxinmian or whatever the dealer has that's been doing well locally. Cotton needs a lot of pesticide — bollworm is the main enemy. I'll spray three or four times: herbicide before planting, then insecticide two or three times during summer, and maybe fungicide if the weather is wet. I also put plastic film down to keep the moisture and heat. I'll topdress with compound fertilizer at flowering in July. Irrigate twice — once in June if it's dry, once in August when the bolls are filling. The problem with cotton is labor. Picking starts in September and goes into October, and you have to pick three or four times as the bolls open. That's why I only keep 6 mu of it — any more and we'd need to hire too many people. Even now I'll probably hire 10-12 days of labor just for picking. I expect about 450 kg per mu of seed cotton.

**Money** — All together, seed, fertilizer, pesticide, water, and film will run me about 10,500 yuan this year. That's a lot of cash to put out at once. I have some savings from last year, but I watch every yuan. I thought about putting more nitrogen on the wheat, but fertilizer prices are up and I'd rather have cash in hand in case something goes wrong. The wheat-maize system is my bread and butter — it's stable. The cotton is my gamble for better income, but only as much as we can pick ourselves.
